artists.biography:
Robert Lee "R. L." Burnside (November 23, 1926 – September 1, 2005), was an American blues singer, songwriter, and guitarist who lived much of his life in and around Holly Springs, Mississippi. He played music for much of his life, but did not receive much attention until the early 1990s. In the latter half of the 1990s, Burnside repeatedly recorded with Jon Spencer, garnering crossover appeal and introducing his music to a new fanbase within the underground garage rock scene.
One commentator noted that Burnside, along with Big Jack Johnson, Paul "Wine" Jones, Roosevelt "Booba" Barnes and James "Super Chikan" Johnson, were "present-day exponents of an edgier, electrified version of the raw, uncut Delta blues sound."

perplexity.description:
A Ass Pocket of Whiskey is the seventh studio album by American blues musician R.L. Burnside, originally released in 1996 on Fat Possum Records. The album is a distinctive fusion of raw Mississippi hill country blues and garage rock, shaped by Burnside's collaboration with the Jon Spencer Blues Explosion. This partnership brought a gritty, energetic edge to Burnside's traditional blues sound, blending electric guitar riffs, driving rhythms, and Burnside's signature growling vocals. The result is a record that straddles genres, appealing to both blues purists and fans of alternative rock.

Within Burnside's discography, A Ass Pocket of Whiskey stands out as a pivotal release that helped introduce his music to a broader, younger audience. The album features a mix of original compositions and reimagined blues standards, showcasing Burnside's deep roots in the Delta blues tradition while embracing a more experimental, rock-influenced approach. Tracks like "Goin' Down South" and "Snake Drive" exemplify this hybrid style, with hypnotic grooves and raw, unfiltered energy.

Critically, the album received mixed but generally positive reviews. While some blues purists were divided—evidenced by contrasting ratings in The Penguin Guide to Blues Recordings—the album was praised for its authenticity and innovation. Pitchfork awarded it a 7.7/10, highlighting its unique blend of tradition and modernity. Commercially, it solidified Burnside's reputation as a vital figure in contemporary blues and helped cement Fat Possum Records' status as a label championing raw, unvarnished Southern music.
